analysis.one_liner: Bars the largest online platforms from buying startups and potential competitors.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced in November 2021 by a Democrat and a Republican acting together, never got a hearing or vote in the Senate Judiciary Committee and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill says that very large online platforms — those with 50 million or more U.S. users, run by companies worth more than $600 billion, and acting as essential gateways for other businesses — may not buy other companies at all. The platform could escape the ban only by proving, with clear and convincing evidence, that the target is tiny (under $50 million), isn't competing with it, and doesn't strengthen its market position. It shifts antitrust enforcement for these deals from the usual case-by-case weighing to a near-flat prohibition, with triple damages for anyone hurt by a violation.
analysis.who_benefits: Small businesses and app developers that sell through the big platforms, startups that could grow into competitors instead of being bought, and consumers who could see more competition, lower prices, and more choice. Enforcement would come from the FTC, the Justice Department, state attorneys general, and private suits.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Small sellers, startups, and platform users

how_it_helps.text: It makes it unlawful for a designated covered platform to acquire the stock or assets of another company, with only narrow exceptions the platform must prove itself.

The bill treats competition for a user's attention as protected competition, and says that simply acquiring more data can count as strengthening a platform's market power — closing two loopholes that let large platforms buy emerging rivals.

Anyone injured by a forbidden acquisition can recover triple damages plus attorney's fees, and state attorneys general can sue on behalf of their residents, giving small firms and states real enforcement tools.
The FTC and DOJ would jointly issue enforcement guidelines within a year and update them at least every four years, so the rules are public rather than case-by-case.

analysis.who_pays: The handful of companies running platforms at or above the bill's size thresholds — companies with net sales or market capitalizations over $600 billion, which in practice means the largest U.S. technology platforms. They would lose the ability to grow by acquisition. Startups and their investors also lose a common exit: selling to a large platform is one of the main ways young companies and venture funds cash out, and this bill closes that door for deals involving covered platforms.
analysis.who_pays_short: The largest tech platforms and their acquisition targets

drawbacks.text: The ban is a bright line rather than a weighing of pros and cons. Some acquisitions genuinely combine products in ways that help users, and this bill would block those too, unless the platform can prove a narrow exception by clear and convincing evidence — a high legal bar.
Blocking acquisitions removes a common way for startups and their investors to be paid back, which could reduce venture funding for new companies in affected markets.

Covered platforms appeal designations and enforcement orders only to the D.C. Circuit, a single court, and the agencies' factual findings are treated as conclusive on review — provisions that consolidate the platforms' legal exposure in one favorable-to-government forum and limit their ability to challenge agency decisions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — keeping dominant platforms from buying out competition before it becomes a threat — addresses a real, widely criticized pattern in digital markets, and the enforcement tools are strong. The cost is real too: a flat ban with narrow, hard-to-prove exceptions will stop some deals that would have been harmless or helpful, and it removes a standard payoff for startups and investors. Whether that trade is worth it depends on how much weight one gives to future competition versus today's deal-making; the bill clearly chose the former.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee on November 4, 2021, and the committee took no further action on it before the Congress ended in January 2023 — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Amy Klobuchar, a Democrat, and Sen. Tom Cotton, a Republican, jointly introduced the bill on November 4, 2021.
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day, and that was the last action ever recorded on it.
It drew three cosponsors — two Senate Republicans and one Senate Democrat — and never advanced out of committee before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The largest technology platforms are better off: they keep the ability to buy competitors and potential rivals, which this bill would have taken away. Lawmakers who preferred no action also avoided a vote on it.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was split across party lines from day one — a Democratic sponsor and a Republican co-introducer, with two Republicans and one Democrat joining as cosponsors — but the bill stalled in a Democratic-led committee without a recorded vote, so no roll call shows how the full chamber stood.

industries.industry: Large online platforms (companies with $600B+ market cap, e.g. the biggest U.S. tech firms)
industries.note: The bill prohibits these companies from acquiring any other company, ending their main tool for absorbing competitors and locking in dominance. Their interest in continuing to buy rivals runs against the small businesses and users who would gain from a more contested market.

Selling to a large platform is a common exit that returns money to founders and investors; a flat ban on those sales removes that payoff for deals with covered platforms, which could cool funding for new entrants. The bill's bet is that more startups will stay independent and grow instead.

industries.industry: Small businesses and developers selling through the platforms
industries.note: These businesses depend on platforms they cannot negotiate with; the bill gives them and state attorneys general triple-damage suits against acquisitions that strengthen a platform's grip over them.
